Fold the EX divider into six registered iterations
motivation:
The bench baseline scores 12.12 at 5.442 MHz. Its reported 199.837 ns,
156-cell path runs through forwarding and the EX ALU to the data-memory
address cone. The ALU places signed and unsigned division and remainder
operators on the same result path as ordinary address arithmetic. A shared
iterative divider should remove most of that depth and reduce LUT use. A
baseline Verilator trace with both bus stalls enabled reproduced 4491485
marker-bracketed cycles with canonical CRCs and retired zero divide or
remainder instructions inside the bracket. Both retired DIVUs were outside it.

On launch, capture the forwarded operands, take unsigned magnitudes for signed

remainder from registered state. Return all ones for a zero-divisor quotient

with zeroed side-effect controls. Capture the actual source values at launch

RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS use the existing four stand-in expressions with the same
launch and completion schedule so formal still exercises the interlock and
forwarding within its existing depth.

bus stall sequence seen by the loop. Compare Gowin's median Fmax and measured

implementation_notes:
# Six-tick EX divider

`DIV`, `DIVU`, `REM`, and `REMU` share a restoring divider. Launch captures the forwarded operands as unsigned magnitudes and records the result kind and sign correction. A 36-bit stream starts with four leading zeros. Each of the next six clocks consumes six dividend bits and shifts six quotient bits into the same register. EX releases the divide when EX/MEM accepts the registered result, adding seven cycles per operation.

The recurrence handles a zero divisor by shifting ones into the quotient and preserving the dividend magnitude in the remainder. Launch suppresses quotient sign correction for this case and preserves the dividend sign for signed remainders. The 32-bit magnitude and sign correction also give `INT_MIN` and zero for the quotient and remainder of `INT_MIN / -1`.

An older stalled data-memory request delays launch. Once launched, the divide holds the PC and ID/EX, lets older instructions drain, and sends bubbles with cleared controls into EX/MEM. Fetch readiness has no effect on execution or result acceptance. EX saves the launch operands for RVFI. The ALTOPS build captures the existing stand-in expression at launch and uses the same six-tick interlock.

## Local verification

- Verilator lint passed with real arithmetic and with `RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS`.
- `make test TARGET=bench` passed all five runners and 81 cocotb cases. Divider coverage includes exact RV32M results, a held result, consecutive requests, reset in flight, and a WB-forwarded operand behind a stalled load. The pipeline tests also cover fetch stalls through result acceptance and forwarding into dependent consumers.
- `formal/run_all.sh` passed all 53 checks on the first run, including all four divide and remainder checks and liveness. Local formal used ALTOPS. Native arithmetic was checked by cocotb and cosimulation.
- `make cosim TARGET=bench` passed selftest RVFI comparison with and without stalls and validated the canonical CoreMark CRCs with both stalls enabled.

## Local performance

| Metric | Baseline | Divider |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Median Gowin Fmax (MHz) | 5.442 | 34.631 |
| CoreMark cycles between markers | 4,491,485 | 4,491,485 |
| Gowin logic cells, placement option 0 | 12,312 | 2,731 |
| CoreMark iterations per second | 12.12 | 77.10 |

The three Gowin placements measured 34.910, 34.631, and 34.631 MHz. The cycle ratio was 1.000, so the stated Fmax gate remained approximately 5.69 MHz. The placement-option-0 critical path is within the six-step divider recurrence, from the registered divisor to the remainder register, with a 33.939 ns data arrival time.
lesson: - 2026-11-22 hyp-20261122-001-r1s0 (regression, +536.14%): Moving combinational DIV/REM off the EX address path into a shared restoring divider raised median Gowin Fmax from 5.442 to 34.631 MHz, and the seven extra cycles per operation left the CoreMark cycle count unchanged because all divides retired outside the timed interval.

title: Move DIV and REM into a bounded multicycle execute unit
motivation: The bench baseline places at a median 5.442 MHz. Its 199.837 ns worst path crosses forwarding and the execute ALU before reaching the data-memory path, and the mapped path contains 156 cells. The four combinational division and remainder operators feed the same result mux as every base ALU instruction and effective address. The path depth makes this arithmetic the strongest candidate for the current frequency limit. An RV32IM reference run of the canonical 2K, ten-iteration, -O3 CoreMark build matched all expected CRCs and retired zero DIV, DIVU, REM or REMU instructions among 2,922,016 instructions between the timing markers.

Move DIV, DIVU, REM and REMU out of the combinational ALU into a single blocking divider attached to EX. On issue, capture the forwarded operands, operation and sign flags. Advance the unsigned quotient and remainder four dividend bits per cycle using two cascaded radix-4 digit steps. Each step uses parallel widened subtracts and their borrow bits to select the residual for the largest fitting multiple of the divisor. In the eighth update cycle, select the quotient or remainder, apply sign correction and transfer directly to EX/MEM. Preserve the specified zero-divisor and signed overflow results. Use the same issue, wait and completion schedule under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS, substituting the specified operand formulas for the arithmetic so the formal gate exercises the same interlocks. The eight extra cycles leave one cycle for a preceding load-use or redirect bubble within the unchanged ten-cycle liveness window when both buses are ready.

Issue only when the older MEM transaction can advance, insert EX/MEM bubbles while waiting and transfer the saved instruction and result exactly once. Report the captured source operands in RVFI and make the completed result available to the next instruction through normal EX/MEM forwarding. Base integer and multiply instructions retain their existing stage latency. The divider adds eight cycles per dynamic divide or remainder and replaces the deep single-cycle division cone with a registered recurrence. The reference profile predicts zero direct divider stalls inside the timed window. Recheck marker-window cycles under the prescribed bus backpressure, since any divide before the start marker can shift the stall sequence. At equal measured cycles, the candidate needs a median routed Fmax above 5.69 MHz to beat the champion and approximately 8.16 MHz to realize the estimated gain.

implementation_notes:
# Bench multicycle divider

`div_unit.sv` implements DIV, DIVU, REM and REMU with two cascaded radix-4 steps per update cycle. Each step uses three parallel widened subtraction results to choose a quotient digit and the next remainder. The result transfers directly to EX/MEM on the eighth update. If the consumer is blocked on that cycle, the divider holds the final step's inputs so the result and operands stay stable. Divide by zero and signed overflow use the same schedule as other operands. ALTOPS uses the specified formulas on the captured operands with the same controller.

EX keeps the instruction in ID/EX and captures the forwarded operands separately for the divide and RVFI. Issue waits for older data memory traffic to advance. EX/MEM receives bubbles while the divider runs, so older instructions can retire. The completed divide transfers once and forwards through EX/MEM. Base integer and multiply operations retain their one-cycle EX latency.

The divider tests live in `test_div_unit.py` so the clocked divider and the combinational ALU can be tested as separate Verilator top modules. `core.sv` includes `core_pkg.sv` when the build has yet to read it, which lets the requested alphabetical glob lint command resolve pipeline types.

## Local verification

- Verilator `-Wall` lint passed in hardware and ALTOPS modes.
- The stock single-channel `bash formal/run_all.sh` passed 53 checks on the first run, including liveness and all four divide and remainder instructions. The script ran in an isolated project copy under `$TMPDIR`.
- All 72 cocotb cases passed across six runners. The divider tests checked 1,188 operation and operand combinations, held completion, and reset. The pipeline tests checked RVFI operands and order, dependent results, older memory backpressure, and retirement gaps of ten cycles after a load-use or redirect bubble on ready buses.
- `NRET=1 make cosim TARGET=bench` passed five ELFs. Selftest and three random traces matched the ISS with ready and stalled buses. CoreMark passed CRC and UART validation with the prescribed stalls.
- The baseline and candidate both took 4,491,485 cycles between the CoreMark markers with the prescribed backpressure. `NRET=1 make fpga TARGET=bench` reported routed Gowin frequencies of 46.428, 45.562, and 45.562 MHz, a median of 45.562 MHz, and fitness of 101.44 CoreMark iterations per second.

The final divider step and sign correction came within 0.002 ns of the worst reported path in placement option 0. Divides add eight cycles each in workloads that execute them.
lesson: - 2026-11-22 hyp-20261122-002-r1s1 (improvement, +736.96%): Two cascaded radix-4 steps with parallel subtracts kept EX division to nine cycles at a median routed core Fmax of 45.562 MHz, leaving one cycle for a load-use or redirect bubble within the ten-cycle ready-bus RVFI liveness bound.

title: Predict direct control transfers in fetch with a bimodal table
motivation:
The benchmark core fetches sequentially until EX resolves a taken transfer.
Its unregistered IF/ID bundle means each nonsequential transfer discards one
fetch slot. Predicting hot loop branches and direct jumps can reuse those
slots for useful work. The measured 156-cell critical path is in forwarding
and the ALU, so the new fetch logic has timing headroom if its fanout stays
local.

implementation_notes:
# Direct control-transfer prediction

Fetch uses a 64-entry table of two-bit saturating counters indexed by `pc[7:2] ^ pc[13:8]`. A resettable validity bitmap selects the backward-taken, forward-not-taken default until the first outcome initializes the entry to weakly taken or weakly not taken. Independent table reads let fetch and training use the pre-update state on the same clock edge.

Fetch predecodes legal conditional branches and JAL and uses one PC-relative target adder for both. It selects a direct target only when the instruction enters ID/EX and the target is word-aligned and below `0x00100000`. JALR resolves in EX. EX compares the registered fetch PC with the resolved successor and redirects on a mismatch in either direction. The same resolved successor feeds RVFI. Alignment traps retain the sequential successor and suppress the link write.

An older dmem hold freezes fetch and EX together and suppresses training and recovery until EX can advance. Recovery then takes priority over imem backpressure and load-use holds. The RTL follows the proposed pipeline organization and adds a guarded declarations include in `core.sv` so the requested wildcard-order Verilator lint command can resolve the bundle types.

## Local verification

- Verilator lint passed with `-Wall`. All five cocotb suites passed, including directed checks for folded-index aliasing, training across a dmem hold, counter saturation, both directions of recovery, and suppression of wrong-path store requests.
- `formal/run_all.sh` passed all 53 single-retire checks on the first attempt. The register check took 135 seconds. The run used a private copy of the existing harness and upstream framework under `$TMPDIR`.
- `make cosim TARGET=bench` passed the self-test RVFI comparisons with and without memory stalls and the stalled CoreMark CRC check.

## CoreMark and Gowin

The stalled CoreMark interval fell from 4,491,485 to 4,190,281 cycles, yielding 7.19% more iterations per cycle. Gowin placements measured 5.375, 5.468, and 5.468 MHz. The 5.468 MHz median and measured cycle count yield 13.05 iterations per second versus the locally reproduced baseline of 12.12, a 7.70% increase. The worst setup paths still cross forwarding and the EX ALU.

Placement option 0 used 12,883 logic cells and 653 registers, up 571 logic cells and 193 registers from the baseline. The logic increase exceeds the scratch estimate. All three placements fit.
lesson: - 2026-11-22 hyp-20261122-003-r1s2 (regression, +7.67%): A 64-entry bimodal table and early JAL target selection in IF avoided taken-transfer bubbles and cut stalled CoreMark cycles by 6.7%, with the combinational DIV/REM path limiting median Gowin Fmax to 5.47 MHz and throughput to 13.05 iterations/s versus 101.44 for the multicycle-divider winner.

implementation_notes:
# Execute-cycle redirect fetch

IF now drives the resolved EX target onto both the instruction address and the IF/ID PC tag independently of bus readiness. It computes the sequential and target increments in parallel. The PC register takes target plus four when ID accepts the instruction and saves the target for retry when acceptance is blocked.

The hazard unit invalidates the IF/ID response when the instruction bus stalls. An instruction-bus stall alone lets the redirecting instruction advance, and a stalled older memory operation holds ID/EX. The existing load-use bubble, divide hold, and EX misalignment checks apply.

The RTL follows the proposed design. The pipeline harness now drives address-specific instruction stalls and samples the fetch address after the ready signals settle. Five directed cases cover ready buses, each bus stalled alone, and both release orders when both stall. Each case checks taken BNE, JAL, and JALR for target retry and acceptance, RVFI PC continuity, and wrong-path exclusion. The ready-bus JAL-to-REMU gap is nine cycles.

Same-cycle target acceptance depends on the combinational instruction response defined by the bus contract. The worst reported paths across all three local placements went to data memory.

title: Register M-extension results separately from fast execute
motivation: The bench champion runs the canonical stalled CoreMark window in 4,491,485 cycles at a median 45.562 MHz. In placement option 0, the worst path runs through a multiplier DSP to a data-memory address input. The divider's final two radix-4 steps and sign correction are within 0.002 ns of that path. In options 1 and 2, forwarding and redirect feed back through the instruction NOP mux and hazard comparison into ID/EX. These paths suggest splitting EX outputs by when they become ready and carrying pipeline validity separately from payload data.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Give the M-extension a late-result lane across the existing EX/MEM boundary. Compute four parallel signed 17-by-17 limb products in EX and register them with the multiply operation. Zero-extend both low limbs. Sign-extend the high limb only for an operand that the operation treats as signed, and zero-extend it otherwise. In MEM, sum the products at offsets 0, 16, 16 and 32 modulo 2^64 and select the requested half. Pass through bits 15:0 of the low-low product. Compress three 48-bit terms with one carry-save layer and one carry-propagating addition. The first term concatenates bits 31:0 of the high-high product with bits 31:16 of the low-low product. The other two terms are the sign-extended cross products. For DIV and REM, carry the raw magnitude and sign-correction flag through the same boundary and apply the conditional negation in MEM. Keep the current divide issue and eight update cycles, including zero-divisor and signed overflow handling.

Register the selected result in MEM/WB alongside the retirement metadata. Interlock an immediately following instruction when either raw instruction source field matches a nonzero late destination, as the ISS compares both RVFI source fields. After one interlock cycle the consumer takes the result from MEM/WB. Independent instructions keep the existing issue rate, and ordinary integer producers still bypass from EX/MEM. Source data-memory outputs from the fast execute lane. Feed raw fetch bits into decode and the interlock, qualifying the comparison with imem readiness and the producer's valid bit. Clear ID/EX validity on a redirect or dependency bubble and qualify downstream side effects by valid. This removes redirect from the path through the instruction bits and interlock.

Keep older dmem backpressure ahead of EX advancement and retain MEM/WB forwarding data through a hold without retiring twice. Keep ALTOPS on the same issue, result and forwarding schedule using the specified substitute arithmetic. Verify the ten-cycle ready-bus RVFI liveness bound for load-to-divide, multiply-to-divide, divide-to-divide and redirected divide sequences. Check that stalled memory requests and single-channel retirement each complete once.

# Page-local direct transfer prediction

IF predecodes legal B and JAL instructions and shares an 11-bit word-index sum for targets within the source page. The speculative select requires an aligned, nonsequential displacement and a source PC below `0x00100000`. A 32-entry direction table uses `PC[6:2] ^ PC[11:7]` and a resettable validity bitmap. # Bench core banked branch target buffer

## Implementation

- Fetch indexes four 16-row banks with `PC[7:2]`. Each bank checks the `PC[19:8]` tag and the direction counter locally, then masks its 18-bit target word address. Fetch selects the OR of the masked targets only for an accepted, legal branch, JAL, or JALR response in the low 1 MiB.
- EX compares the current fetch address against the target and PC+4 in parallel. A mismatch squashes the younger instruction and registers the appropriate recovery pulse. The next cycle uses the correction for both the imem request and the instruction's PC tag, and saves that address for retry when fetch is blocked. A misaligned taken transfer resumes at PC+4 with the trap set and the link write suppressed.
- A valid, advancing control transfer with aligned, in-range source and target addresses queues one registered update. Each bank reads its old tag and direction counter at write time. Conditional branches allocate weakly taken, saturate on subsequent matches, and update the target on taken outcomes. JAL and JALR record strongly taken. Bank validity and update validity reset, and simultaneous fetches see pre-write contents.

## Implementation choices

- Each bank uses separate tag, direction, and target arrays. The training port reads the old tag and counter, and a separate write enable preserves the target on a not-taken outcome.
- Fetch registers the normal PC select alongside the two recovery pulses. Prediction, sequential advance, and retry feed the PC through a one-hot selection. This shortened the fetch path that limited the first Gowin build to a 74.454 MHz median. The worst placed paths in the revised build end at the divider result registers.
- A changed control transfer with a stale entry can incur repeated recovery when its new target is misaligned or outside the cacheable range. Each recovery uses the exact architectural successor.

title: Decouple instruction fetch with a four-entry fall-through queue

among the longest routed paths, so the queue needs a short invalidation
path and independent payload write enables.

# Four-entry fall-through fetch queue

## Implementation

- Fetch stores each queued instruction with its full PC and the prediction used to advance the request. One-hot occupancy, head, and write-slot registers control the circular queue. Decode sees the live response when empty. Fetch advances on instruction readiness and registered space availability. Each payload write enable uses the registered write slot and registered occupancy only.
- Decode acceptance accounts for data-memory holds, divider holds, and late-result dependencies. Both raw source fields of the selected packet feed the interlock and forwarding, including when an instruction-bus stall leaves a queued packet at the head.
- EX uses byte-parallel branch comparisons, immediate bit 1 for direct-transfer alignment, and bit 1 of the two-bit JALR sum. A shared, advancing direction-mismatch signal invalidates queue control and squashes ID/EX. The existing registered target and fall-through selects drive the recovery request. A blocked request is retained in the split normal PC for retry.
- Pipeline tests assert empty-queue latency, full-queue hold, wraparound with simultaneous push and pop, drain during an instruction-bus stall, queued dependencies on either raw source, and retention of a queued jump's prediction. The recovery tests check both redirect directions with updated fetch traces and retain the retirement, retry, and exact data-memory checks.

## Verification

After changing it to a signal width, `pc_fwd_ch0` reported an expected successor of `0x0000000c` followed by a retirement at `0x00000000`. The trace and synthesis log showed Yosys writing single bits of an unpacked array of packed structs. The second retry fixed the elaboration by declaring each slot as an explicit packed vector.

title: Let branch prediction run two fetches ahead of decode
motivation: The bench champion's page-local predictor runs only when decode accepts the current fetch. A data-bus hold, divide, or late-result dependency can stop the predictor from consuming a ready instruction even though the instruction bus is independent. Buffering the predicted path lets fetch use those cycles and gives decode ready instructions to consume during later instruction-bus stalls.

hypothesis.motivation: The bench champion's page-local predictor runs only when decode accepts the current fetch. A data-bus hold, divide, or late-result dependency can stop the predictor from consuming a ready instruction even though the instruction bus is independent. hypothesis.hypothesis:
Put a two-entry fall-through queue between the existing page-local predictor and decode. For every accepted imem response, compute the predicted successor at the current fetch PC and advance the fetch cursor. If decode can accept the live response and the queue is empty, bypass it directly to ID/EX. Otherwise retain the instruction, its full PC tag, and the prediction bit that actually steered fetch. Route the oldest entry to decode and shift a valid tail to the head on dequeue. Accept another ready response whenever a slot is free or the head issues that cycle. A full queue with a blocked head holds the fetch cursor and both entries. Use a separate enable for the tail payload so it samples the live packet whenever the effective tail is empty or decode is unblocked. Update tail validity from imem readiness when a valid tail shifts to the head or when blocked decode leaves a valid head and an empty tail. In all other cases retain the effective tail validity. This keeps the enqueue decision off the wide tail register enable. An unready instruction bus prevents a new enqueue while valid queued instructions remain available to decode. Use the selected decode instruction's validity and raw source fields for the late-result interlock.

On an advancing EX misprediction, squash the younger ID/EX input with the existing EX pulse. Use the registered recovery select to mask both queue valid bits in the next cycle, so the correction fetch sees an empty queue and can bypass if ready. The stale queue entries are discarded as that recovery cycle completes. Keep the selected correction PC for retry if the instruction bus stalls, and predict from the correction PC on acceptance. Qualifying the queue with the registered select keeps the EX comparison off its payload enables. Prediction updates still come from valid, advancing, nontrapping EX branches, including when subsequent fetches are stalled. Each queued instruction keeps its original prediction even if the direction table changes before decode. Preserve the existing one-cycle miss penalty with ready buses, precise traps and links, and ordered single-channel retirement.

The two-entry queue reduced stalled CoreMark to 3,978,219 timed cycles, 5.89% below the champion's 4,227,283. With the separate tail payload enable, Gowin measured 88.224, 90.511 and 90.511 MHz, using 4,738 LUTs and 1,290 registers in option 0. At the measured cycle count this gives 227.52 iterations/s, up 5.78% from 215.09. The replacement margin requires a median above 89.504 MHz. The divider result path limited both median placements, leaving about 1 MHz of margin for implementation and routing differences.

The timed prototype passed the canonical CoreMark CRC and marker checks, all six cocotb suites, and the self-test and three random RVFI traces with and without bus stalls. The ready-bus formal liveness and both PC continuity checks also passed.

The radix-16 divider selects its 32-bit residual through four levels of binary muxes. # Implementation notes

The RV32M divider selects its schedule at issue by testing the signed or unsigned divisor against the nonzero magnitude range below `2^20`. The threshold test runs in parallel with the byte-wise input negation. The narrow schedule uses the leading-nibble setup and seven 24-bit radix-16 updates. The recurrence stores only the low 20 remainder bits and transfers the seventh update directly to EX/MEM. The even fit thresholds select one of eight pairs, and the odd threshold selects the residual within that pair.

The wide schedule seeds the remainder with the top 20 dividend bits and resolves the remaining three digits in two cycles each. It shares the low 24 bits of the trial subtractors with the narrow recurrence and computes the upper byte for either borrow. Each full candidate and its fit bit are registered before one-hot reduction. The fit bit checks every multiple bit above bit 31. Divide by zero follows the same completion schedule with a saved dividend magnitude or an all-ones quotient. The issue-to-transfer timing is shared by hardware and ALTOPS. The result and original RVFI operands hold through completion backpressure, and MEM applies the result sign.

The four-entry fetch queue now invalidates its contents by setting a single empty flag on redirect. The next queued packet starts at the current write slot. # Implementation notes

MEM registers a replay observation for each completing instruction, including the resolved direction of deferred branches. A 32-word circular history tracks page-local sequential runs and identifies a span from the displacement of a short taken backward branch. Observations continue during a copy. The registered reader advances through the captured span before the writer can wrap onto it. One synchronous replay RAM holds both 16-word banks. Installation publishes the full head PC with the final write, prefers an empty bank before round-robin replacement, and protects the active bank or the matching idle head. Each bank keeps its first packet in a register. The idle read primes the second packet and the replay cursor advances only on enqueue.

The four-entry fetch queue decodes from a dedicated registered head and keeps three rear slots. A one-entry pop can replace the head directly. With rear entries present, promotion takes the oldest rear packet while the incoming packet takes the free rear slot. The ordinary bus path retains empty-queue fall-through. The interlock reads the source fields and aligned-branch flag from the live instruction or the registered head and qualifies them with the masked EX valid.

The resolving edge registers the correction, its MEM origin, and FENCE.I invalidation. The next cycle ignores the stale queue head and cancels ID/EX work. A MEM-origin correction also masks EX/MEM before any memory request, forwarding, training, or retirement. The older MEM correction preserves the recovery address captured during the branch's EX cycle and the branch retains its saved retirement slot. The correction pulse resets the divider before the target can issue. A ready correction fetch uses a sequential prediction. A stalled correction is copied into the normal PC for retry. An advancing FENCE.I refetches its successor after older memory completes and clears replay state, including an in-flight installation.

The directed pipeline tests cover both replay admissions, two banks at the same page offset, a 16-word body, simultaneous promotion and enqueue, deferred side exits, correction stalls, and divider cancellation with a divide at the corrected target. They also cover an older MEM miss with a younger store, branch, JALR, or FENCE.I, and FENCE.I invalidation of resident and partially installed loops. The folded counter probes exercise the predictor on normal fetches, including a read on the same edge as a counter write.

The configured single-retire formal run (`FORMAL_WORK_ID=R12s2streamdec`) passed 52 of 53 checks within the local budget, including cover, liveness, and both PC consistency checks. # Radix-16 divider implementation

The divider captures the dividend magnitude and a signed 33-bit negative divisor on issue. Four independent byte additions perform conditional negation. The leading-nibble update uses a captured positive low nibble and a greater-than-15 flag computed directly from the input divisor.

Setup forms the seven negative odd multiples with 37-bit shifted terms and carry-save reduction. The original monotone residual mux tree and quotient encoder select the final result.

The leading-nibble calculation differs from the proposal. A four-case decode handles the first two bits, followed by two restoring steps in the same setup cycle. A ready bus response can fall through to decode. On a stall, an exact hit with queue space advances the PC and enqueues its instruction and prediction together. The existing EX and deferred MEM correction paths validate replayed transfers, and the correction cycle uses the bus.

Gowin initially mapped wide tag equality onto a carry chain. Two-bit comparison groups let it map the full tags in parallel. # Source-first fetch prediction and registered recovery

## RTL changes

Fetch selects the live or replay branch and JAL qualifiers, cold direction, target word, and folded target index using `imem_ready` in parallel with the direction table read. ID/EX captures the prediction bit and independently qualifies aligned, non-deferred branches for EX correction. EX compares the registered prediction with the actual direction. The addresses and selector are captured at the existing EX boundary and selected during the existing IF correction cycle.

The load comparison, alignment traps, wrong-path valid masking, and retirement edges retain their existing behavior.

The directed suite checks that a ready bus response overrides conflicting replay steering and that an unready bus response carrying a JAL cannot steer an accepted replay.

title: Learn loop exits and publish the next direction before fetch
motivation:
CoreMark repeatedly exits loops whose back edges stay strongly taken in
the 64-entry bimodal table. A scratch predictor that remembers repeated
taken-run lengths reduced stalled CoreMark from 3,379,213 to 3,356,526

bottleneck was the path from the resolved branch index through the loop
state update into the fetch prediction bit. Separately registering the
read, transition, and publication can shorten that path.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Retain the 64-row folded word-PC index. Each row tracks a saturating
six-bit count of taken outcomes since the last exit, the last completed
count, and whether two consecutive completed counts matched. Trust counts
from 3 through 62. For a trusted trip, predict an exit when the current
count reaches the learned length, and drop confidence if the branch runs
past it or exits early. Use a two-bit saturating fallback that records
agreement with the backward-taken default. At reset the fallback starts
weakly in agreement.

Train once on a valid nontrapping conditional branch completion in MEM,
using the resolved outcome including for load-dependent branches. Pipeline
update capture, metadata read, and state transition. If a captured update
reads a row with an older unpublished update, restart the sampled state
so the younger sample cannot extend a stale trip. Publish state
and one precomputed direction-override bit together. Reset the trained
map, override bits, and update valids. Keep the count, trip comparison,
and confidence logic on the training side.

Fetch reads the override bit from four 16-row banks in parallel using
a replicated four-bit row register per bank. Load every replica with
the normal-PC write enable, including recovery, and preserve the
replicas through synthesis to confine lookup fanout to each bank.
Latch the one-hot bank select separately so bank selection adds no
row-register enable logic. Construct the fall-through or taken
successor bundle for each possible override value in parallel.
Each bundle contains the next word PC and its folded lookup index. Both
use the instruction sign and the existing target eligibility for live
and replayed instructions. Let the override select the final bundle and
predicted-taken bit. Keep the existing correction priority and EX/MEM
validation.

A scratch version with a shared row register, pipelined training, and
late successor selection validated the canonical CRCs at 3,363,240
marker cycles and matched the ISS on selftest and three random programs
with ready and stalled buses.
It reached 103.434 MHz median across three Gowin placements, with the
median limit in the existing late load-to-branch compare. Its 307.54
iterations/s falls short of the 312.39 champion. Loading only the
selected bank's row in a separate trial added a fetch control path and
reduced the median to 96.346 MHz at the same cycle count. At that cycle
count the tournament margin requires a median above 109.90 MHz. The
gain estimate assumes the replicated lookup with a shared enable can
reach that frequency in the routed core.
